props.title: Such a Gorgeous Kid Like Me
props.initialSlug: Dark comedy about a seductive female killer

sections.content: François Truffaut's darkly comedic **Such a Gorgeous Kid Like Me** (1972) marks a fascinating departure from his more celebrated works like **The 400 Blows** (1959) and **Jules and Jim** (1962). This twisted character study follows Camille Bliss, a manipulative young woman telling her life story to a naive sociologist. The film showcases Truffaut's experimentation with noir elements and black comedy, while maintaining his signature exploration of human nature. It shares DNA with later femme fatale narratives like **Basic Instinct** (1992) and **Gone Girl** (2014), though with Truffaut's distinctly French New Wave sensibilities. movies.title: Such a Gorgeous Kid Like Me
movies.slug: A criminology student interviews a manipulative young woman in prison, becoming entangled in her web of deception

sections.content: The film represents a crucial pivot point in Truffaut's career, coming after his more experimental 1960s work but before his return to more conventional narratives with **The Story of Adele H.** (1975). Bernadette Lafont's magnetic performance as Camille draws from the same well of complex female characterization that would later influence films like **Amelie** (2001) and **Elle** (2016). Truffaut uses his documentary-style framework to deconstruct the femme fatale archetype, creating something more nuanced than typical noir offerings. SUBHEAD: The New Wave Connection

While less discussed than contemporaneous works like Godard's **Tout va bien** (1972) or Rohmer's **Love in the Afternoon** (1972), **Such a Gorgeous Kid Like Me** demonstrates how French New Wave directors were evolving beyond their revolutionary 1960s approaches. The film's blend of true crime elements with comedy predates similar genre hybridizations in works like **To Die For** (1995) and **I, Tonya** (2017).
